items.title: I tried to move my notes out of Emacs. I failed. Again.
items.author: Jack Baty
items.content:
Every so often I suffer from what I call "Emacs Fatigue". It's closely related to "Text File Fatigue". Using Emacs tends to pull one toward using it for everything, which is what I'd done. Then, I simply grow tired of staring at the same thing every day. When this happens, I "decide" to uproot my life and move my notes into something else. This time, that something else was Bear.

Bear is great. It's solid, beautiful, and refreshingly simple. It syncs flawlessly (for free) and runs on macOS and iOS. It's also inexpensive. It uses an SQLite database, which doesn't bother me. Databases are great at this stuff. All the "But but what if the database...?!" talk is mostly hearsay anyway.

The thing that made me twitchy was that it felt like my notes were "in there". It's not the database. It's the fact that everything is in an app, and that app makes me need to use that app. This is how I'd started to feel about Emacs, but mostly due to Org mode.

Bear is macOS and iOS only, which should be fine for someone like me who has "decided" to live on macOS. And yet, Linux continues to emit a low-grade hum in the back of my head that I can't ignore.

If I don't want my notes in Org mode files, but I'm still drawn toward Emacs, what should I do? Denote! That's where they'd all started in the first place, but as .org not .md. I'd nearly forgotten that Denote handles Markdown files natively. One Emacs configuration change and I was back where I belong. And since Bear notes are already Markdown, all it took was an export and a (Claude Code-assisted) conversion script for file names, links, and attachments.

So yes, I've done that thing where I quit using Emacs only to come crawling back later. I know better, but knowing better doesn't stop me. Maybe I'll work on a sync/bridge between Denote and Bear. That would be neat.

items.title: Tuesday, October 6, 2026
items.author: Jack Baty
items.content: A couple of weeks ago, I moved all of my Denote (Org mode) notes into Bear app on my Mac. I was feeling trapped by Org mode. I was tired of always having to convert from .org to .md and back again, so I made the call to go all-in with Markdown, via Bear. Then I changed my mind. Instead, I changed Denote to use Markdown rather than org-mode. That's better. More on this later.

items.title: Moving my social identity to littleFedi
items.author: Jack Baty
items.content:
I liked the software immediately. It was fast, simple (considering all the features), and easy to install.

I put up a poll on Mastodon asking if I should just go for it and migrate to littleFedi or should I post something on Mastodon pointing to the new handle. Within just a few minutes I had enough votes (13 to 0) in favor of fully migrating that I went for it.

The nice part is that I'm in complete control of the software that my Fediverse identity runs on. The scary part is the same as the nice part.

items.author: Jack Baty
items.content:
what struck me about Gurman’s article is just how unenthused I am by an Apple smarthome product. Some of this is fatigue from a decade of Siri disappointment and skepticism about the company’s ability to deliver on a voice-centric product. More than that, however, I bristle at the idea of introducing Apple’s constraints to more parts of my life.

I've been surprised that I feel much the same way.

items.title: My brain on a Sunday morning
items.author: Jack Baty
items.content:
I was on my Mac this morning, just minding my own business, when suddenly I found myself using the Linux laptop, and I liked it.

On Sunday mornings, I do system maintenance. This means running updates on all my computers. Right now, that's five machines: one Linux desktop, two Linux laptops, one Mac desktop, and one Mac laptop. Yes, that's too many, but it is what it is.

Both Linux laptops run CachyOS, which is Arch-based, so there are updates.

I started with the Framework. Once it was updated and rebooted, I pulled the latest tweaks to my Emacs config, to make sure it worked on Linux. I've been leaning toward using macOS exclusively, so I haven't been testing things on Linux as much. Everything worked, though.

While typing on the Framework, the first thing I thought about was how much I prefer typing on it to typing on the MacBook Air. Then I remembered how much I like the of Linux. Then I noticed that Emacs starts up more than twice as fast on the Framework for some reason. Then I remembered that the best (and only) way to have consistent Emacs key bindings on Linux is to, well, use Emacs.

All this to say that the conflict between running macOS, Linux, or both is still a thing. As troublesome and complex as it can be, I think the answer will always be "both". Surely I can manage it, right? Maybe if I only use the laptops for simple things like blogging, browsing, or journaling, things will be easy enough. I'll never be able to settle on one or the other. Just admit it.

I'm on the couch typing this in Emacs using the Framework, both things I told myself a week ago that I'd stop doing. My stupid brain is always mucking things up.

items.title: littleFedi
items.author: Jack Baty
items.content:
littleFedi is "A small ActivityPub server written in Go"

A few years ago I'd decided I wanted to "own my content" 🙄 so I ran an instance of Mastodon. Mastodon is overkill and I didn't enjoy it. Then, later, I installed an instance of Go2Social, which worked well. Trouble was, I was all-in with social media at the time and being on a single-user instance felt lonely...nothing useful in "local" or "trending". Discovery was difficult. It was just me and I didn't like it.

Fast forward to today, and things have changed. I've deleted all of my Meta-related accounts and LinkedIn. I thought about quitting Mastodon as well, but FOMO always gets the better of me.

Since I would rather not quit Mastodon completely, I figured I would try running a single-user instance again. Maybe the quiet would be good for me.

I'd seen @Stefano's posts about a new ActivityPub server he was working on and the timing of the first release couldn't be better, so I installed it today at Jack Baty Social.

It's running on my Hetzner VPS behind Caddy as a proxy. I love Caddy. Here's the entire Caddy config for the domain:

social.baty.net {
	encode gzip
	reverse_proxy 127.0.0.1:8081
}

I've just started poking around, but littleFedi seems like it's got a lot going for it. At first I wanted to use my root domain for my handle () but since I'd previously used that via Ghost, I ran into caching issues and didn't want to bother, so now I'm @jack@social.baty.net.

The big question is whether to migrate followers there, or start fresh and maybe just announce the move from my main @jbaty@social.lol account. I think I'll give it a minute before deciding.

littleFedi is a compelling new entry in the FediverseSpaceArena.

items.title: Friday, October 2, 2026
items.author: Jack Baty
items.content: Sal's follow-up to my post about ending my Linux experiment includes a note about Apple Messages. I can't believe I didn't mention that. One of the biggest drawbacks for me on Linux was not having easy access to Messages. (Nearly) everyone I correspond with uses Messages. I hate typing anything on my iPhone, so having to switch to my phone to text someone was no fun at all. And forget about sharing a funny meme or whatever. I could never get KDE Connect, LocalSend, and friends to work fast enough or consistently enough to make it worth it. It was one hurdle I was never able to clear when using Linux.
